questions.q: What problem does a clustering key solve?
options: It replaces the need for a primary key on a table
It encrypts a column's values automatically
It permanently sorts a table's physical row order on disk
It keeps a column's values co-located across micro-partitions as a large, frequently updated table changes, so pruning stays effective
questions.explain: As tables grow and get updated heavily, values for a given range can scatter across many micro-partitions. A clustering key tells Snowflake to actively keep them co-located, keeping pruning useful.

options: A one-time operation that never needs to repeat
A setting that clusters every table in the account automatically by default
A free process that runs instantly with no compute cost
The background process that reorganizes micro-partitions to match a table's clustering key, consuming background compute credits
questions.explain: Automatic clustering runs in the background to maintain a clustering key's co-location as data changes, and it costs background compute credits — which is why it's reserved for large tables that actually need it.

questions.q: What makes the result cache return a query almost instantly, as shown in this lesson's screenshot?
options: The exact same query text ran before and the underlying data hasn't changed, so Snowflake returns the cached result at zero compute cost
The warehouse was resized to XXL just before the second run
A clustering key was applied to every column
The query was rewritten to remove all joins
questions.explain: The result cache holds query results account-wide for 24 hours; an identical query against unchanged data returns instantly from cache without spinning up any compute.

questions.q: What can the metadata cache answer without needing a running warehouse?
options: User authentication requests
Any arbitrary SELECT query with joins and filters
Pruning decisions and simple aggregates like COUNT(*), from stored statistics alone
Row-level data updates
questions.explain: The metadata cache holds per-micro-partition statistics like min/max and row counts in the cloud services layer, which can sometimes answer pruning decisions and simple aggregates without warehouse compute.

questions.q: What happens to the warehouse (local disk) cache when a warehouse suspends?
options: Nothing changes; local disk cache is unaffected by suspension
It is preserved indefinitely regardless of suspension
It disappears — a resumed warehouse starts with a cold local disk cache
It gets automatically promoted to the result cache
questions.explain: The warehouse cache lives on that warehouse's local SSD while it's running. Suspending the warehouse clears it, so a resumed warehouse has to re-read data from cloud storage until its cache warms up again.
